newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe considers setting up secondary bond market.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe considers setting up secondary bond market.

text.p: Zimbabwe's central bank said on Wednesday it was working towards the establishment of a secondary bond market, and was currently considering setting up an association of market makers in government securities.

But Joyce Zhakata, assistant general manager for money and capital markets in the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ), told a seminar the current trading patterns on the local primary stock market would have to change before this happened.
The one-day conference, organised by Bard Discount House of Zimbabwe, was attended by officials from commercial and merchant banks, building societies, discount houses and stockbrokers.

Zhakata said their ideas should help move the plan ahead but gave no timetable of when Zimbabwe hoped to have a secondary bond market. But she said the RBZ was reviewing a number of key issues impeding the process.

The impediments, Zhakata said, included the mandatory requirement for insurance and pension funds to hold 55 percent of their assets in government primary securities which currently, out of Z$10.5 billion ($983 million) worth of stocks on issue, has only left Z$4.2 billion available for trade.

"It is therefore worthwhile that this ratio be reviewed with a view to gradually reducing or removing it altogether," she said, pointing out there was also a need to address current restrictions on secondary market trading by foreign investors which has ruled out their participation on the primary market.

"In this regard the government and the RBZ will review the issue in order to attract and mantain foreign participation in our market as rational investors can only participate in a market where stocks can easily be bought or sold depending on cashflow needs," she said.

Zhakata said the development of a secondary market had also been hindered by the range of instruments on offer, saying there was a need to consider introducing new instruments such as zero coupon bonds and index-linked stocks.

This move, she added, would also require local investors -- whom she said were currently generally happy to buy and hold onto securities -- to trade aggressively so as to improve liquidity in the market.

In moves towards the secondary bond market, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe and the government were currently amending and drafting new banking, securities and exchange acts, and also looking at setting up a central depository to manage the clearing and settlement of transactions in securities, she said.
